items.title: EU advances Syrian recovery and reconstruction through Syria Partnership Coordination Forum in Damascus
items.blurb:
Country: Syrian Arab Republic
Source: European Commission

Please refer to the attached file.

Today, the Syria Partnership Coordination Forum (SPCF) convened in Damascus for the first time to advance Syria's recovery and reconstruction, showcase investment opportunities and agree on concrete steps forward.

The SPCF brought together key partners, including EU Member States, the G7, Arab countries, and the UN and International Financial Institutions, such as the World Bank, the European Investment Bank, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development and the Islamic Development Bank, as well as civil society, to discuss Syria's business environment and steps to translate Syria's priorities into concrete investment opportunities.

The Forum, co-chaired by Syria and the EU, was opened by Commissioner for the Mediterranean Dubravka Šuica and the Syrian Minister of Foreign Affairs, Assaad Al-Shaibani.

Economic revitalisation, institutional recovery and improved livelihoods

In her second visit to the country, Commissioner Šuica officially launched the Syria Technical Assistance Hub to support Syrian institutions in strengthening their capacities and advancing reforms that are instrumental to restore confidence, attract responsible investment and support sustainable economic recovery.

The Commissioner also witnessed the signing of new EU-funded contracts supporting Syria's recovery and reconstruction, namely on the rule of law, on an enabling business environment andon support to small and medium-sized enterprises. These initiatives will help revive the economy, strengthen public institutions and improve livelihoods. By helping businesses access finance and grow, the projects can create jobs and improve conditions for investment. They will also improve access to justice, supporting a recovery that benefits people across Syria.

During her bilateral meeting with Minister Al-Shaibani, Commissioner Šuica received Syria's signed undertaking to implement the EU's Registered Exporter system. This marks an important step towards enabling Syrian products to benefit from preferential access to the EU market under the Generalised Scheme of Preferences, opening up new opportunities for Syrian exporters and supporting the country's economic recovery.

Commissioner Šuica also visited the Deir Ali Power Plant together with Ibrahim Al-Adhan, Syrian Deputy Minister of Energy and EIB Vice President Gelsomina Vigliotti. The visit highlighted the importance of restoring Syria's energy infrastructure for economic recovery and explored opportunities for future EU engagement in the energy sector with other international partners.

Background

After the fall of the Assad regime at the end of December 2024 and following the Brussels IX Conference of 17 March 2025, Syria and the EU launched the SPCF, which provides a platform to align partners' support on Syria's recovery priorities and coordinate on their implementation.

The Forum is instrumental in facilitating structured engagement among key partners, including EU Member States, the G7, Arab nations, and International Financial Institutions. The SPCF is structured under regular senior-official plenary meetings at capital level, and regular practical level.

It builds on the EU's support for Syria's recovery. During her first visit to Damascus in June 2025, Commissioner Šuica announced €175 million to help Syria rebuild its institutions, advance transitional justice and revive its economy. items.title: Humanitarian Coordinator calls for strengthened Ebola readiness in South Sudan
items.blurb:
Country: South Sudan
Source: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs

Please refer to the attached file.

Juba, 17 November 2026 – The United Nations Resident Coordinator and Humanitarian Coordinator in South Sudan, Mr. Ramanathan Balakrishnan, has called for increased preparedness and readiness to respond to a potential Ebola virus disease (EVD) outbreak in the country.

The call follows a recent full-scale simulation exercise conducted in October 2026 by the Ministry of Health, the National Public Health Institute (NPHI), the World Health Organization (WHO) and partners to assess the country's capacity to detect, notify, investigate and respond to a potential EVD outbreak.

The exercise assessed key areas of South Sudan’s Ebola preparedness efforts, including case management, infection prevention and control, laboratory capacity, contact tracing and coordination. While the exercise demonstrated the system’s capacity to quickly detect simulated cases, significant gaps remain in alert management, rapid response team management, health worker remuneration, ambulance services, laboratory facilities, personal protective equipment supplies, contact tracing, and screening arrangements at points of entry.

To address these challenges, the Humanitarian Coordinator has launched a three-month prioritised plan to mobilise financial resources to address the operational and capacity gaps identified during the simulation exercise. He called on donors and partners to support the plan, which requests USD$7 million to strengthen preparedness and response capacities.

“While there are no reported cases of Ebola in South Sudan, closing these preparedness gaps is critical to ensure that South Sudan is better prepared to detect, contain and respond to a potential outbreak, and to protect the lives and well-being of its people,” Mr. Balakrishnan said.

Reiterating the importance of national government leadership in strengthening EVD preparedness, Mr. Balakrishnan said, “The payment of health worker salaries by the government authorities is critical, as is facilitating access for Ebola-related movements for both health actors and UNMISS and ensuring the safety and security of humanitarian workers.”

items.title: World: ACNUR presenta un nuevo portal de datos sobre refugiados para reforzar la evidencia e impulsar soluciones para millones de personas desplazadas
items.blurb:
Country: World
Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

GINEBRA – En un momento en el que la información fragmentada y la narrativa sesgada sobre el desplazamiento forzado corren el riesgo de influir en decisiones que afectan a millones de personas, ACNUR, la Agencia de la ONU para los Refugiados, presentó hoy su nuevo Portal de Datos sobre refugiados, un punto de acceso único y abierto a datos fiables y verificados sobre personas refugiadas, desplazadas por la fuerza y apátridas.

Por primera vez, el portal recopila estadísticas demográficas junto con información sobre las condiciones de vida, las necesidades de protección y la situación socioeconómica de las personas desplazadas, ofreciendo una visión más completa del desplazamiento, su magnitud, los retos a los que se enfrentan las personas y los avances que se están logrando hacia la búsqueda de soluciones.

Desde datos sobre la pobreza y la matriculación escolar hasta la nutrición, el acceso al agua potable y otros indicadores de bienestar, el portal ofrece una visión más amplia de lo que significa que una persona esté desplazada.

“Detrás de cada dato hay una persona, una experiencia vivida y un futuro. Disponer de datos fiables es esencial para garantizar que las decisiones que tomamos protejan la seguridad de las personas, respeten su dignidad y les brinden oportunidades para prosperar”, afirmó Edem Wosornu, Alta Comisionada Auxiliar para la Protección de ACNUR.

En consonancia con la visión “50 para 35” de ACNUR, cuyo objetivo es reducir a la mitad el número de personas desplazadas por la fuerza que dependen de la asistencia humanitaria para 2035, esta base empírica más amplia ayudará a los gobiernos, a los socios para el desarrollo y a las organizaciones humanitarias a medir los avances hacia la autosuficiencia y las soluciones, evaluar si las políticas y los programas están mejorando la vida de los refugiados, identificar las desigualdades persistentes y las deficiencias operativas, y determinar dónde se necesitan más medidas e inversiones.

Por ejemplo, los datos comparables sobre pobreza disponibles a través del portal para diez países muestran que las tasas de pobreza entre las personas refugiadas superan sistemáticamente a las de las comunidades de acogida, oscilando entre alrededor del 10 por ciento y más del 90 por ciento en los datos recopilados entre 2018 y 2024.

Gracias a una experiencia de usuario moderna e integrada, el Portal de Datos sobre refugiados de ACNUR permitirá a los usuarios explorar, acceder, reutilizar e integrar los datos en sus propios análisis, informes y procesos de toma de decisiones.

Periodistas e investigadores pueden recurrir a información fiable para investigar tendencias, situar las cifras de desplazamiento en su contexto, y elaborar reportajes y análisis basados en pruebas. El nuevo portal permitirá la integración de los datos sobre desplazamiento en sus otras plataformas, mapas, informes y herramientas digitales a través de interfaces de programación de aplicaciones (API) abiertas.

El portal también está diseñado para funcionar con otras plataformas de datos, incluido el Sistema de Datos Comunes de las Naciones Unidas, lo que crea oportunidades para conectar datos sobre personas refugiadas con estadísticas de desarrollo más amplias y comparar las circunstancias de los refugiados con las del conjunto de la población en ámbitos como educación, empleo, salud, financiación y otros aspectos de la vida.

El lanzamiento del portal también supone un paso importante en la transformación digital más amplia de ACNUR. Mediante la consolidación de sistemas de datos fragmentados y la adopción de estándares de datos modernos, la automatización y la inteligencia artificial, la organización pretende que su infraestructura de datos sea más predictiva, eficiente y capaz de responder a las necesidades actuales.

“No se trata solo de una actualización tecnológica, sino de una inversión estratégica en un enfoque más sostenible, adaptable y eficiente de la gestión de datos, que reduce la fragmentación y facilita el mantenimiento, el desarrollo y la mejora de los sistemas a lo largo del tiempo”, afirmó Wosornu. “En última instancia, el Portal de Datos sobre refugiados de ACNUR se basa en una convicción sencilla pero poderosa: la información fiable puede cambiar la forma en que el mundo entiende el desplazamiento y cómo responde ante el”.

Al situar los datos y las pruebas fiables en el centro del debate mundial sobre el desplazamiento forzado, ACNUR pretende reforzar la confianza, respaldar políticas e inversiones más eficaces y contribuir a que una comprensión más profunda del desplazamiento se traduzca en acciones duraderas y significativas.

El Portal de Datos sobre refugiados se ha desarrollado con el apoyo del Centro Conjunto de Datos sobre Desplazamiento Forzado del Banco Mundial y ACNUR.

Nota para editoras y editores:

La versión actual del Portal de Datos sobre refugiados incluye un conjunto limitado de funciones y contenidos. La plataforma seguirá desarrollándose en 2027 y, con el tiempo, se irán añadiendo conjuntos de datos, páginas por país y contenidos temáticos adicionales. Como parte de este proceso, los portales de datos existentes de ACNUR se irán retirando progresivamente en los próximos meses.

items.title: ‘I Thought I Was Bad at Art’: How a Museum Is Changing the Way Children See Their Creativity
items.blurb: “I felt that there were opportunities to draw and participate in school activities, but there were fewer chances for children to showcase their work to a wider audience.” For 18-year-old Sahil Santosh Kundojwar, art was something he enjoyed creating but mostly shared with teachers, friends, and family. He had opportunities to draw at school, but finding an audience beyond his immediate circle was not easy. That changed in July 2024, when a teacher at The Aditya Birla Public School in Awarpur, Maharashtra, introduced him to the Children’s Art Museum of India (CAMI). He submitted a drawing of Ganpati Bappa for a theme called ‘My Superhero’. It won a prize, giving him the encouragement to share more of his work. “I didn’t expect to win a prize, so receiving recognition for my Ganpati artwork was a very special and motivating experience for me,” he says. His story reflects the idea behind CAMI, a digital museum that gives children a dedicated space to display their artwork. Founded in January 2022 by cousins Krish Nawal and Manya Roongta, the platform has grown to more than 3 lakh registered members. Its collection includes over 20,000 artworks, and the website has received more than a million visitors from over 200 towns and cities. The idea began with a question the siblings found themselves asking during COVID-19. Children were creating art at home, but where could they go to have it seen, appreciated, and preserved? A museum of their own During the pandemic, the siblings were spending more time at home and creating art themselves. They noticed that children around them were doing the same, but much of this work stayed in school notebooks, folders, or at home, with few opportunities to reach a wider audience. Founded in January 2022 by cousins Krish Nawal and Manya Roongta, CAMI has grown to more than 3 lakh registered members. They felt that children’s artwork should not be limited to occasional displays at school exhibitions or relegated to a corner of a museum primarily meant for adults. They wanted to build a space where young artists would be at the centre. Krish recalls the question that set the idea in motion. “Why wasn’t there a space where a child could say, ‘This is my artwork, and it belongs in a museum’?” Krish, now 16 and a Class 11 student at The Shri Ram School in Gurugram, and Manya, 19, who is pursuing a bachelor’s degree in the United States, began working on the idea together. For the 16-year-old, the aim was to change how children viewed their own creations. “I wanted to create a space where children could see their artwork displayed, feel that it mattered, and know that it deserved to be seen,” he says. Manya wanted the experience to feel different from uploading an image online. “We did not want to create just another website where children could upload pictures. We wanted the artwork to have a context and a sense of recognition,” she tells The Better India . Turning that idea into a functioning museum meant learning almost everything from scratch. The siblings began with an Excel spreadsheet, mapping out how children would submit their work and how the museum would organise and display it. They experimented with WordPress and Wix to build early versions of the website and emailed schools and children to gauge interest. There was no established organisation or technical team behind them. They learnt about website development, communication, curation, and outreach as they went along, with their parents helping them through the early stages. “The first step was deciding that we were going to build it rather than keep talking about it,” Krish says. The website went live in January 2022. Its first version was uncomplicated, allowing children to submit artwork and have it displayed in an online collection. The first submission was a picture of a peacock sent in by a young child. Because the website did not yet require all the details it collects today, the founders knew very little about the artist. They have even tried to trace her since. Krish remembers the submission for what it represented. “There was just a child who had created something and wanted a place to share it,” he says. Where young artists find recognition As children began finding the platform, CAMI grew beyond its original digital collection. The founders started introducing programmes that would give young artists regular reasons to create and share their work. One such initiative is the monthly ArtFest. Each edition revolves around a theme or creative prompt, which children can interpret in their own way before submitting their artwork. Selected entries are showcased as part of the programme. For Krish, the aim was to change how children viewed their own creations. The idea is to encourage participation rather than make creativity depend on winning a competition. Manya says the team wanted children to have opportunities to return to the platform and keep experimenting. “We realised that children should not have to wait for one opportunity to submit their artwork. We wanted our initiative to give them regular reasons to create, participate, and explore,” she says. CAMI also works with schools through dedicated galleries , ArtFests, and other creative initiatives. These programmes allow students to display their work beyond the classroom. Its collaborations include Sarvodaya schools in Delhi, the Aditya Birla Group, and Bagiya Foundation. Children aged three to 18 can submit their artwork through the website. Each entry goes through a verification process to ensure it is appropriate for children. Art teachers, curators, and members of the core team review submissions, generally within 24 to 48 hours. The team considers originality, effort, and creative expression rather than expecting professional-level technique. Accepted artwork becomes part of the digital collection or may be considered for an ArtFest, exhibition, or school gallery. Children also receive a CAMI certificate. “We are not looking for technical perfection. A child’s artwork does not need to look professionally executed to have value,” explains the teen founder. The museum has also developed a learning section with resources on creating, appreciating, and understanding different art forms. These include traditional and indigenous Indian styles such as Warli, Madhubani, and Pattachitra. Children and visitors can also engage with CAMI through its YouTube channel and Spotify podcast. In 2023, the founders took the museum into another digital environment by launching a virtual museum on Roblox. With more than 120 million daily active users globally, the platform offered a way to reach children in a space where they already play, create, and connect. The virtual museum allows players to walk through galleries and view artwork made by children. It has received over 2,70,600 visits, extending the reach of the collection beyond the conventional website. What recognition can mean to a young artist? For the founders, the value of the initiative is not measured only through membership figures or the number of artworks in its collection. Some of the most meaningful moments have come through the responses they receive from children. Manya remembers an Instagram message from a girl who was around 12. After seeing her painting displayed in the museum, the child wrote, “I used to think I wasn’t good at art, but when you displayed my painting in the museum, I began to feel that maybe I was,” she recalls. The founders started introducing programmes that would give young artists regular reasons to create and share their work. The message stayed with the co-founder because it showed how being taken seriously could change a child’s perception of their own ability. “She was not suddenly a professional artist, and nothing about her artistic ability had changed overnight. What changed was that someone had taken her work seriously enough to give it a place,” she says. Manya has also seen how children’s creative expression changes as they continue making and sharing art. Some begin with familiar drawings of two mountains and the sun, but gradually experiment with portraits, posters, different compositions, and styles such as cubism and modern art. “For me, that progression is not really about becoming a ‘better’ artist in a technical sense. It is about becoming more confident in having an idea of their own and being willing to experiment with it,” she says. Seventeen-year-old Kritika from Delhi has experienced some of that encouragement herself. Before joining CAMI in September this year, she mostly shared her artwork with family or during school art classes. She wanted to see her work displayed alongside that of other children and hoped for feedback that would help her take herself seriously as an artist. Her first submission, titled ‘Fish Illusion’, was accepted for the online gallery. Seeing it published encouraged her to begin working on another project. “When I first submitted my artwork on the website, I hoped that my work would be accepted and displayed on a real platform. I wanted to see how it looked alongside other children’s art and hoped to get some encouragement or feedback that would make me feel like a real artist,” she says. Her parents’ response to the painting also stayed with her. They complimented her use of colours and told her that the artwork had brought a smile to their faces. “That made me realise that my art has the power to make people happy,” she adds. Having her work displayed on the platform has made her more comfortable sharing it with others. “Now, I feel incredibly proud to show people my work and confidently call myself an artist,” she says. Sahil, too, explains that the recognition he received through CAMI made him more confident about putting his work forward. Appreciation from teachers and classmates after winning the Monthly Best Prize encouraged him to participate in more activities. He has one piece of advice for young artists. “I would tell them not to be afraid or shy about showing their work. If you are proud of what you have created, you should share it with others because your creativity is special and unique . Don’t worry about whether everyone will like it,” he says. Building a community across India As the initiative developed its programmes, its reach began extending beyond the founders’ immediate circles. What started with children from familiar schools and communities now includes participants from major cities as well as smaller towns and villages. CAMI also works with schools through dedicated galleries, ArtFests, and other creative initiatives. The founders cite participation from places such as Vaniyambadi, Rampurhat, Guntur, Nainital, Khammam, Ranaghat, Patna, Bareilly, Nagpur, Coimbatore, Kanhagad, Prayagraj, Kota, and Puducherry. The platform has also reached villages in Uttarakhand and smaller communities in West Bengal and Odisha. Manya says the geographical spread has been one of the most surprising aspects of the journey. A digital museum, she explains, allows a child from a smaller town to participate in the same collection as someone living in a major city. The first major sign that CAMI was gaining momentum came by June 2022, when the team began receiving artwork submissions every day. Its first school collaboration showed the founders that they could reach groups of children through educators, rather than relying only on individual submissions. The Roblox museum, launched the following year, opened another route to young audiences. The initiative now has a core team of five members, supported by more than 20 volunteers and over 500 young brand ambassadors. It continues to operate as a bootstrapped initiative, with the founders relying on their own resources and family support rather than institutional venture funding. Their roles have changed as the museum has grown. Krish, who initially handled everything from the website and social media to school outreach and submissions, now focuses more on its development, operations, and future direction. Manya’s responsibilities centre on ideation, marketing, outreach, and programme development. Building the initiative while studying has also taught them to manage their time and share responsibilities. Krish works on the initiative after school and during weekends, while prioritising academics during examinations. As the team has expanded, he has learnt to delegate rather than remain involved in every task. “I often say that school taught me how to learn, but CAMI taught me how to turn ideas into something real,” he says. The siblings are now looking at ways to create more opportunities for young artists. These include exhibitions, local art initiatives led by ambassadors and avenues through which children can have their artwork commissioned. The co-founder sees this as a natural next step for a platform built around recognising young people’s creativity. Children aged three to 18 can submit their artwork through the website. “If we tell children that their creative work has value, we should also think about how we can create real opportunities around that value,” he says. From an Excel spreadsheet and a simple website to a community of more than 3 lakh registered members, CAMI has grown considerably since 2022. At its core, it continues to champion the idea that children’s creativity deserves to be taken seriously , giving young artists the encouragement and recognition to keep creating. All pictures courtesy CAMI.
